demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette:
Ravi was a 52-year-old South Asian man who had come to describe his life as split into “before” and “after,” though he struggled to say what the latter was for anymore. He worked as a maid in a hotel, moving through guest rooms with the same practiced efficiency he had relied on for years, and he kept up the appearance of steadiness by arriving early, speaking little, and finishing his work before anyone could ask how he was doing. That order had begun to unravel after an accident months earlier, when he had been helping move a heavy cart in a narrow corridor at work and, in a moment of poor judgment and haste, lost control of it. The cart struck a guest hard enough to cause a serious injury. Ravi could still see the event not as a continuous story but as a handful of brutal snapshots: the corridor light reflecting off the floor, the guest turning too late, the sudden impact, and the look on the man’s face. He described each moment as if it were a picture fixed in his mind, and when one of those images rose up unexpectedly, it would come back with such force that he was immediately back in the corridor, flooded with the same heat and anger he had felt at himself and at the chaos of that instant.

Those memories did not stay neutral. Ravi had come to believe that the accident revealed something unforgivable in him. He said he had acted in ways that went against who he was, that he was not the careful man his family and coworkers had trusted, and that the event happened because of the way he acted. The more those frozen scenes returned, the more they seemed to condemn him. He no longer felt that his life had any meaning, and he spoke about work, home, and even his divorced life as if all of it had been drained of purpose. What remained was a harsh conviction that he had ruined another person’s life and, in the process, damaged whatever good had once defined his own. The shame was not abstract; it sat with him whenever he folded linens or wiped down a sink, because those ordinary tasks now felt like proof that he was only pretending to be the kind of man he once believed himself to be.

Over the following weeks and months, Ravi began guarding himself against anything that might call up those pictures without warning. The hotel corridor, the clatter of a cart wheel, a sudden shout from down the hall, even the sight of someone stepping quickly out of a doorway could set off the memory before he had time to brace himself. At work, he started taking slower routes and keeping to quieter floors, arranging his day so he would not have to pass the narrow service corridor where the accident had happened. At home, alone in his apartment after the divorce, he kept the television on low volume for background noise, partly to avoid being left alone with the pictures in his mind. Yet the harder he worked to keep them away, the more they seemed to define him. When one image broke through, the rage on recall was immediate and intense, and with it came the familiar certainty that he had failed in a fundamental way. He found himself replaying the moment again and again, not in search of relief but in search of an answer for why he had been so reckless, why he had not been better, why he had done something that still felt to him like a betrayal of his own values.

By the time he came for help, the burden had begun to affect the shape of his days. He was still showing up to work, but the effort of keeping the memories at bay left him tense and preoccupied, and he had started to notice how much of his life was now organized around avoiding reminders of the accident. What brought him to treatment was the fear that the pictures in his mind were taking over everything, and that the emptiness he felt was not temporary but the truth of who he had become. He wanted to know whether he could ever stop seeing that corridor, stop blaming himself, and find a way to believe that his life still held something worth living for.
